name: Chandragupta Maurya
role: Founder of the Maurya Empire, remembered in Jain tradition as a monk-king
summary: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire around 320 BCE. Digambara Jain tradition says he gave up his throne, became a monk under Bhadrabahu and fasted to death in Karnataka.
about: Chandragupta Maurya ruled from Magadha in the late 4th and early 3rd century BCE and is usually credited with founding the Maurya Empire. No record written in his own lifetime describes his conquests, so historians stitch his story together from Greek and Roman writers and from Jain, Buddhist and Hindu texts composed much later. Those texts disagree about his family and how he beat the Nandas. Digambara Jain tradition says that in old age he handed the kingdom to his son, followed the teacher Bhadrabahu to the south and ended his life by sallekhana on Chandragiri hill at Shravanabelagola. Some scholars accept this and others doubt it. Jains still honour the memory at the Chandragupta Basadi there.
kidSummary: Chandragupta Maurya was a young man who became the first emperor of a huge kingdom in ancient India, about 2,300 years ago. Greek visitors wrote about him and called him Sandrokottos. Jain stories say that when he was old he gave up his crown and became a quiet monk in the hills of Karnataka.

story.title: A boy who played king
story.text: In Buddhist and Hindu stories, a wise teacher named Chanakya sees a boy, Chandragupta, playing king with shepherd friends and giving orders like a ruler. Chanakya takes him in and trains him to rule.

story.title: A kingdom is built
story.text: Chandragupta gathers an army, defeats the Nanda kings of Magadha and builds an empire with its capital at Pataliputra.

story.title: Friends with Greeks
story.text: He faces Seleucus, the Greek ruler on his north-west border. They make peace: Chandragupta sends 500 war elephants and gets land, and Seleucus sends an envoy named Megasthenes.

story.title: A warning of famine
story.text: Digambara Jains say a teacher named Bhadrabahu foresaw a twelve-year famine. Chandragupta, they say, gave the throne to his son and followed him.

story.title: A quiet end on the hill
story.text: Tradition says the old king lived as a monk on Chandragiri in Karnataka and fasted peacefully, in the Jain way of sallekhana.

teaches: Letting go of power and wealth
Leaders can choose peace over conquest
emblems: Peacock (in Buddhist tales of his name)
texts: Writings of Strabo, Justin and Plutarch

facts.text: Greek writers called him Sandrokottos or Sandracottus. In 1793 William Jones matched that name to Chandragupta, a link that became the anchor for dating ancient Indian history.
The Greek writer Justin says a wild elephant came and offered itself as his mount, and that a lion licked him as he slept while on the run. Both were read as signs of his future.
Around 305-303 BCE the Greek ruler Seleucus I made peace with him and handed over land in the north-west. In return, Seleucus received 500 war elephants.
Those elephants helped Seleucus win the battle of Ipsus against Antigonus, which let him build the huge Seleucid Empire.
Megasthenes, the Greek envoy at his court for about four years, credited Chandragupta with a thousand-mile highway linking his capital Pataliputra to Taxila in the north-west.
Buddhist texts link the name Maurya to peacocks, and one even describes a city built of bricks coloured like peacock necks.

In Buddhist and Hindu legends, young Chandragupta played at being king with his shepherd friends and gave orders like a real ruler. Chanakya saw this, bought him from the hunter who kept him and adopted him.

Legend says the beaten Nanda king was allowed to leave Pataliputra alive, riding a chariot loaded with belongings for his household. Jain sources add that his daughter fell for Chandragupta and married him.
Greek writers describe him drinking wine, performing Vedic rites and hunting, while Jain tradition remembers him very differently, as a monk who gave up his throne.
Plutarch reports that Chandragupta saw Alexander the Great as a young man and said later that Alexander nearly conquered the land, because its king was despised for his base character and low birth.
In Hemachandra's 12th-century Jain version, monks could turn invisible to take food from the imperial storehouse, and Chanakya used cunning and force to grow the empire.

One passage in Justin, once read as a meeting between Chandragupta and Alexander, may come from a printing slip. Manuscripts seem to say 'Nandrum', meaning the Nanda king, not 'Alexandrum'. Plutarch's separate sighting of Alexander is not affected.

In a Jain account, Chanakya was foretold to become the power behind an emperor. He helped a peacock-breeder chief's daughter give birth, asked to adopt the boy later, and came back years afterwards to claim Chandragupta.
His son Bindusara followed him as emperor, and Bindusara's son was Ashoka, so the monk-king of Jain memory was grandfather to the great Buddhist emperor.
The earliest text to tell of his fast to death, Harisena's Brhatkathakosa, never mentions the Maurya Empire and has his disciple set out from Ujjain, so some propose a later person of the same name.
Chanakya feared plots, so Chandragupta is said to have changed bedrooms often to confuse conspirators, and on hunts he was ringed by female guards.
In Jain tradition, Chanakya secretly fed Chandragupta tiny amounts of poison so that his body would resist any assassin's attempt. The emperor did not know about it.

In Hemachandra's tale, the emperor once shared his food with his queen Durdhara, who was expecting, and the poison harmed her. A drop of it touched the baby's head, so the child was named Bindusara, from bindu, a drop.

One tradition says the treaty with Seleucus included a marriage alliance. The Rajavamsa and the Bhavishya Purana speak of Chandragupta marrying a Greek princess, though Seleucid writers never mention an Indian match.

Rudradaman's inscription at Junagadh says the Sudarshana lake in Gujarat was made in Chandragupta's reign by his governor Pushyagupta, and that Ashoka's governor later added channels. It shows his rule reached Gujarat.

The Jain text Parishishtaparvan says Chanakya raised Chandragupta's army by minting coins, and made an alliance with a king named Parvataka. Buddhist accounts say the army was recruited after Chandragupta studied at Taxila.

quiz.q: What did Chandragupta give Seleucus in the peace treaty?
quiz.why: He sent 500 war elephants to Seleucus, who used them at the battle of Ipsus, and Chandragupta gained land in the north-west.

quiz.q: Where do Digambara Jains say Chandragupta spent his last days?
quiz.why: Tradition says he lived as a monk on Chandragiri hill in Karnataka.

quiz.q: Which Greek name was used for Chandragupta?
quiz.why: Greek writers wrote Sandrokottos or Sandracottus, which helped historians date him.

quiz.q: Which teacher is said to have guided Chandragupta to the south?
quiz.why: Digambara tradition names the teacher Bhadrabahu.
